title: Triradiate spicules form at three-cell junctions with rays at 120°, four-rayed at ~109°

fields.label: Label
fields.value: Triradiate spicules form at three-cell junctions with rays at 120°, four-rayed at ~109°

fields.label: Statement
fields.value: Skeletal material deposited between cells or within their partitions takes the shape of the cell junctions: in a layer of equal cells, where partitions meet in threes at 120°, it forms triradiate spicules with rays at 120°, and in a solid aggregate of four cells it forms tetrahedral four-rayed spicules with rays at about 109°; unequal cells give unequal angles and curved rays.

fields.label: Notation
fields.value: three equal cells \Rightarrow triradiate spicule, rays at 120^\circ; four cells \Rightarrow tetraradiate, rays at \approx 109^\circ 28'

fields.label: Chapter
fields.value: Ch. IX: On Concretions, Spicules, and Spicular Skeletons

fields.label: Quotation
fields.value: It is plain, accordingly, that in any flattened or stratified assemblage of such cells, a solidified skeletal deposit which originates or accumulates either between the cells or within the thickness of their mutual partitions, will tend to take the form of triradiate bodies, whose rays (in a typical case) will be set at equal angles of 120°

fields.label: Agent
fields.value: delphisci On Growth and Form claim extractor

fields.label: Assumptions
fields.value: D’Arcy Wentworth Thompson, On Growth and Form (1st ed., Cambridge: Cambridge University Press, 1917), Chapter IX, “On Concretions, Spicules, and Spicular Skeletons”; topic “Triradiate and tetractinellid sponge spicules”. Scope: triradiate and tetractinellid spicules of calcareous and tetractinellid sponges

fields.label: Notation
fields.value: three equal cells \Rightarrow triradiate spicule, rays at 120^\circ; four cells \Rightarrow tetraradiate, rays at \approx 109^\circ 28'

fields.label: Assessment
fields.value: GPT-5.6 Sol on thompson1917-ch09-10: partially-resolvable, resolvability 0.59

fields.label: Finding
fields.value: The angular predictions are precise and readily analyzed. Public morphology can test angle distributions, but resolving formation at cell junctions needs rare developmental volumes and controls for crystallography.

fields.label: Proposed test in the assessment
fields.value: Proposed test with existing data: Measure ray angles and curvature in 3D spicules and, where developmental imaging exists, compare ray trajectories with three- and four-cell junctions. Support requires clustering near 120 and 109.47 degrees for equal-cell junctions and predictable deviations with unequal cells.

fields.label: Evidence against
fields.value:
Crystal growth constraints can generate similar angles.

Matched developing-cell and spicule datasets are scarce.

operationalizability: 0.85
data adequacy: 0.35

fields.label: Finding
fields.value: The angles are explicit and distinguish the junction hypothesis from orthogonal or random rays. Large numbers of triacts and tetracts have been figured, but they are not an open measurement dataset, and planar triacts are much easier to score than four-rayed spicules in space. A small team could test the 120 degree case from published images; the tetrahedral and unequal-cell clauses need 3D that is only partly available.

fields.label: Proposed test in the assessment
fields.value: Proposed test with existing data: Measure angles between rays of triradiate and four-rayed spicules. Equal cells should give 120 degree triacts and tetrahedral angles near 109 degrees; a distribution centered on 90 degrees or on no preferred angle would refute the junction rule, and unequal cells should widen that scatter.

fields.label: Evidence against
fields.value:
There is no pre-measured angle table, so the sample has to be compiled from plates.

Most available views are 2D micrographs or drawings, which bias 3D tetrahedral angles.
